title: One came back (Luke 17:11–19)
hookLine: ten lepers healed, and one, a Samaritan, returns to say thank you

lines: SOMEONE CAME BACK TO SAY IT.
cards: A birthday is over, and a parent stands over a child with a pen and a stack of cards: write your thank-you notes. To the child, it's a chore.
A thank-you that arrives days later, unasked, saying what you did for me mattered, is a different thing. Jesus is still on the road to Jerusalem, passing between Samaria and Galilee.
At the edge of a village, ten men stand far off, because their disease means they have to keep their distance.

teach.b: They lift up their voices: Jesus, master, have mercy on us. In the Law of Moses, leprosy names a range of skin conditions, and Leviticus says the person must dwell alone, outside the camp, and cry out that he is unclean.
Jesus doesn't touch them this time. He just says: go, show yourselves to the priests.

That's what the Law required when someone was healed, so the priest could declare them clean and they could go home. And as they went, they were cleansed. Nine keep walking, doing exactly what Jesus told them.
"And one of them, when he saw that he was made clean, went back, with a loud voice glorifying God." He falls on his face at Jesus' feet, giving thanks. And Luke adds: and this was a Samaritan.
The outsider. Jesus asks, almost to himself: "Were not ten made clean? and where are the nine?" He calls the man a stranger, the only one who came back to give glory to God.

Then: arise, go thy way, thy faith hath made thee whole. Here's what a Catholic ear catches. Luke's Greek word for giving thanks is eucharistein, the word behind Eucharist, the name Catholics give the Mass itself.
Some Catholic readers see the Samaritan, face down on the road, as a small picture of that: a healed man who turns around and gives thanks.
They were obedient. They were also in a hurry to get back to their lives.

how: Catholics call the Mass the Eucharist, from the Greek for thanksgiving, and some make a short prayer of thanksgiving in silence after receiving Communion before leaving the church.

o: an outsider from Samaria, the one who came back
a priest who declared the lepers clean
a soldier of Rome posted in Galilee

p: stood far off: master, have mercy
to the priests, as the Law required

s: the ten were healed the moment Jesus spoke
as they went, they were cleansed: healed on the road.
they were doing what he said: going to the priests. only one turned back.
the word Eucharist comes from the Greek for giving thanks
Luke uses the verb for the Samaritan at Jesus' feet.

games.q: you're one of the ten. on the road to the priests, you look down and your skin is clean. what do you do?
o: keep going to the priests, as he said.
games.why: nine keep going. one, a Samaritan, turns back, glorifying God with a loud voice, and falls at Jesus' feet.

practice: Think back over the last month: who helped you, and you kept walking? A doctor, a teacher, a friend who listened, a stranger who held a door at the right moment.
Choose one, and get specific about what exactly they did and what difference it made; if you pray, give thanks to God for them too.

wordCard.voice: Samaritan. Of ten lepers healed on the road, the one who turned around to give thanks was this outsider. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: giving thanks. The root of the word Eucharist.

carryVoice: Your line: where are the nine. Only one stopped long enough to turn around. Until tomorrow.
